summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Clinical diagnosis of tic disorders (TDs) is often delayed by fluctuating symptoms and the subjective nature of assessments. While automated methods have been proposed to bridge this gap, traditional machine learning models frequently lack robustness in unconstrained environments and fail to capture the complex, multisite tics characteristic of severe TDs. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and evaluate a fine-tuned large vision-language model framework for the automated, interpretable detection of pediatric motor tics, addressing the clinical need for objective and efficient symptom assessment in unconstrained environments. <strong>Methods:</strong> In this multicenter study, 168 pediatric participants (n=83, 49.4% with TDs and n=85, 50.6% healthy controls) underwent 12-hour continuous video-electroencephalography monitoring. We fine-tuned the Qwen3-VL-8B model using 3- to 5-minute video segments via low-rank adaptation. The framework used chain-of-thought prompting to generate both binary classifications and textual justifications. A strict patient-wise split ensured zero identity overlap between training and test sets. Diagnostic precision was evaluated using 95% CIs calculated with the Clopper-Pearson exact method. <strong>Results:</strong> In total, 168 pediatric participants (age: mean 8.3, SD 2.3 years) were enrolled, providing 559 expert-validated video segments for analysis. On the independent test set (n=55), the framework achieved 89.1% (49/55; 95% CI 77.8%-95.9%) accuracy and an area under the curve of 0.950 (95% CI 0.892-1.000), significantly outperforming the landmark-based deep neural network (accuracy 74.1%; <i>P</i>=.004); recall reached 100% (25/25 positive episodes; 95% CI 86.3%-100.0%). Model-generated justifications showed substantial agreement with expert annotations (κ=0.784, 95% CI 0.625-0.943; <i>P</i><.001). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> These findings suggest that a vision-language model framework can capture clinically relevant tic features beyond conventional geometric descriptors. By combining high sensitivity (recall) with text-based diagnostic justifications aligned with clinical severity dimensions (eg, frequency and intensity), the approach may support automated video review and preliminary symptom quantification in controlled monitoring settings.
title: Large Vision-Language Models for Pediatric Motor Tic Detection: Case-Control Diagnostic Study

summary: Background: AI has the potential to improve clinical decision-making, efficiency, and patient outcomes, yet adoption in routine clinical practice has been slower than anticipated. While prior studies have identified factors that influence AI implementation, a comprehensive synthesis grounded in implementation science frameworks is lacking. Objective: This study aimed to qualitatively and comprehensively describe barriers and facilitators to AI implementation in clinical care settings using an implementation science determinants framework, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), and to identify AI-specific determinants not fully captured by CFIR. Methods: We conducted an umbrella review of reviews examining determinants of AI implementation in clinical practice. In accordance with the PRIOR (Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Reviews) reporting guidance, we systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL for English-language reviews published between January 2013 and July 2025. Reviews were included if they addressed barriers to and facilitators of implementing AI-enabled digital health tools in clinical care settings. Determinants were deductively mapped to the updated CFIR and inductively analyzed to identify emergent AI-specific constructs. Review quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist, and overlap among primary studies was evaluated using the GROOVE (Graphical Representation of Overlap for Overviews) tool. Results: Twenty-two reviews published between 2021 and 2025 were included, encompassing studies conducted from 1990 to 2025. Reviews varied in design, including systematic, scoping, rapid, narrative, and literature reviews. Overall review quality was mixed, with 9 (41%) reviews rated at 100% quality and 4 (18%) at 50% or lower. Primary study overlap was slight, with a corrected covered area of 0.4%. Determinants of AI implementation were identified across all CFIR domains. Prominent barriers at the innovation level included limited evidence of clinical impact, poor interpretability, complexity, lack of adaptability, and insufficiently representative data. Facilitators included perceived relative advantage, co-design with clinicians, and evidence of local clinical benefit. At the implementer level, low AI literacy, limited confidence, time constraints, and concerns about professional displacement were common barriers, while training and technical support facilitated adoption. Inner setting barriers included inadequate infrastructure, limited resources, poor workflow compatibility, and weak governance structures. Outer setting barriers included unclear policies, laws, and liability frameworks, whereas partnerships and cross-sector collaboration were frequent facilitators. Inductively identified AI-specific determinants included transparency, trust, accountability, model bias, data governance, model maintenance, robustness, generalizability, existential threat, and concern about loss of the human element in care. Conclusions: AI implementation in clinical settings is shaped by complex, multilevel, and AI-specific determinants that extend beyond traditional digital health considerations. Implementation science frameworks can be adapted to incorporate these constructs. Tailored, theory-informed strategies addressing technical, organizational, psychological, and regulatory factors are essential to support safe, equitable, and sustainable integration of AI into clinical care. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD42024501642; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024501642
title: AI-Enabled Digital Health Tool Implementation in Clinical Practice Settings: Umbrella Review

summary: This is a correction of "Detecting and Mitigating AI Bias in Health Care: Development and Validation of a Unified Multistage Framework".
title: Correction: Detecting and Mitigating AI Bias in Health Care: Development and Validation of a Unified Multistage Framework

summary: Background: Despite growing recognition that AI-driven systems offer transformative benefits for diagnostic imaging, insufficient evidence exists regarding how medical imaging workforces adapt to AI technology to support workforce sustainability. Objective: The aim of this study is to systematically review the existing literature on perceptions and attitudes toward AI adoption in medical imaging, postadoption adaptation behaviors within the workforce, and the implications of these processes for workforce sustainability. Methods: Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, a systematic search was carried out across 7 databases. Thematic analysis was used to systematically identify, analyze, and interpret patterns across the literature, providing a comprehensive understanding of workforce perceptions and adaptation behaviors. Results: A total of 69 peer-reviewed articles were included for thematic synthesis. The findings produced 6 critical factors that were identified as themes associated with AI adoption: perceived benefits, trust, readiness to change, autonomy and control, perceived threat to professional identity, and attitudes and intentions toward AI adoption and use. Four key facets of effective cognitive and behavioral adaptation were identified: training and skills development, task performance during AI-assisted practice, reduction of mental health burden and work strain, and policy compliance. The influence of work engagement and job satisfaction on workforce sustainability was also conceptualized. The findings were integrated into a framework describing the radiology workforce perspectives on AI adoption, adaptation behaviors, and workforce sustainability. Conclusions: The findings have potential implications for policy, particularly in strengthening AI-equipped medical imaging systems, fostering trust in AI-driven technologies, and supporting workforce training and upskilling, while considering professional autonomy and role identity. The review highlights a research gap, emphasizing the need for further investigation into postadoption adaptation processes and informing policy development that links AI integration with long-term workforce sustainability in medical imaging.
title: AI Adoption, Adaptation, and Workforce Sustainability in Medical Imaging: Systematic Review and Conceptual Framework

summary: Background: Repurposing approved drugs offers a time- and cost-effective alternative to traditional drug development. However, in silico prediction of repurposing candidates is challenging and requires the effective collaboration of specialists in various fields, including pharmacology, medicine, biology, and bioinformatics. Fragmented, specialized algorithms and tools often address only narrow aspects of the overall problem. Heterogeneous, unstructured data landscapes require the expertise of specialized users. Hence, diverse data sources might not integrate smoothly across workflows. Objective: We aimed to develop an integrated, natural language–driven system that enables domain experts to conduct complex network-based drug repurposing analyses by integrating heterogeneous biomedical data sources and specialized bioinformatics methods within a unified workflow. Methods: With ChatDRex, we present a conversation-based, multi-agent system that facilitates the execution of complex bioinformatic analyses aiming for network-based drug repurposing prediction. It builds on the integrated systems medicine knowledge graph NeDRexDB. ChatDRex provides natural language access to its extensive biomedical knowledge base. It integrates bioinformatics agents for network analysis, literature mining, and drug repurposing. These are complemented by agents that evaluate functional coherence for in silico validation. Its flexible multi-agent design assigns specific tasks to specialized agents, including query routing, data retrieval, algorithm execution, and result visualization. A dedicated reasoning module keeps the user in the loop and allows for hallucination detection. Results: ChatDRex operationalizes complex network-based drug repurposing workflows through conversational interaction, integrating biomedical knowledge access with algorithm execution and validation-oriented assessments. Its modular multi-agent architecture enables scalable task specialization across retrieval, analysis, validation, and visualization, while the reasoning module provides transparency and safeguards against unreliable outputs. Conclusions: By enabling researchers with limited computational expertise to control complex analyses with natural language, ChatDRex could democratize access to bioinformatics as an important resource for drug repurposing. It could enable clinical experts to generate hypotheses and explore drug repurposing opportunities, ultimately accelerating the discovery of novel therapies and advancing personalized medicine and translational research.
title: Conversational Multi-Agentic Network-Driven Disease Module Identification and Drug Repurposing Prediction With ChatDRex: Platform Development Study

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) models have enabled substantial advances across a wide range of healthcare applications. Since the entry into force of the Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) in 2024, these systems have become subject to a common regulatory framework in the European Union intended to harmonize AI governance across all Member States. One of the Act’s distinctive features is that it accommodates existing economic, technological, and regulatory differences among European countries by leaving certain implementation responsibilities to national authorities. This is evident in regulatory sandboxes, supervised environments for developing, testing, and validating AI systems before deployment. In this viewpoint, we propose recommendations for the design of healthcare regulatory sandboxes. These recommendations address the need to document model compression techniques that may affect the classification of large high-risk systems above the 10²⁵ FLOPs threshold, to incorporate explainability into AI systems from the design stage, to identify and document biases in healthcare datasets, to clarify the treatment of federated learning parameter updates under the GDPR, and to strengthen the oversight of AI agents in clinical environments. The implementation timeline makes this discussion particularly timely, given the approaching deadline of 2 August 2026, by which all Member States must have established at least one national regulatory sandbox
title: Rethinking Health Care Regulatory Sandboxes Under the European Union AI Act

summary: In the ongoing AI boom—now supercharged by large language models and generative AI tools—the rapid integration of AI into health care and public health has created an urgent need for professionals who combine deep domain expertise (clinical, epidemiological, ethical, and contextual expertise in health and public health) with AI fluency (the ability to understand, critically evaluate, use, and oversee AI systems effectively). Without domain guidance, AI risks producing biased, unsafe, or contextually irrelevant outputs that compromise patient safety and exacerbate disparities. Conversely, domain experts lacking AI fluency may underuse or misuse these technologies, missing opportunities to improve care quality, operational efficiency, and population health. A foundational understanding of the modern AI system stack—comprising energy, accelerators, infrastructure, models, and applications—empowers health professionals to make informed decisions on adoption, evaluation, governance, and ethical use without needing to code or build models themselves. This stack framework highlights critical interdependencies and health care–specific challenges, including regulatory compliance, data privacy, sustainability, and resource constraints, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This paper argues that cultivating domain-AI bilingualism is essential for safe, effective, and equitable AI integration worldwide. It outlines the 5-layer AI system stack applied to health care, key reasons for hybrid expertise, and a practical 4-step pathway: awakening (recognizing AI’s transformative role), intrepidity (courageously engaging foundational AI concepts), bilingualism (translating between clinical needs and AI capabilities), and visionary leadership (driving organizational and policy readiness). It outlines major barriers, targeted strategies, and recommendations for educators, institutions, and policymakers. By bridging domain knowledge with AI fluency, health professionals can direct—rather than be directed by—AI technologies, including emerging agentic systems, toward more precise, sustainable, and human-centered outcomes while mitigating risks. This hybrid capability represents a nonnegotiable competency for the health workforce for thriving in the post-2026 AI era.
title: Domain Knowledge Plus AI Fluency: The New Nonnegotiable Competency for the Health Workforce in the AI Era

summary: Background: While AI has existed for decades, the introduction of generative AI tools and subsequent advancements in their capability and public use resulted in a shift in public awareness and perceptions of AI. In response, the research community has grown increasingly interested in understanding public perceptions of AI use in various contexts, including health care. Public perceptions shape AI acceptance and consequently integration into health care. It is thus crucial to understand public trust in AI and perceptions of risk as we consider its implementation moving forward. Objective: This study aimed to (1) document the extent of what is known within the literature regarding public perceptions of AI applications in health; (2) interrogate existing definitions and theories of trust being used to guide investigations of public trust in AI; and (3) identify practice and policy considerations and support the design, deployment, and regulation of these technologies in a manner that is trustworthy. Methods: The Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines were used to review publications between 2022 and 2024 across 4 databases, resulting in the inclusion of 41 papers for review. Key findings were then charted and organized into tables to help answer the proposed research questions. Results: Public trust in AI in health care was shaped by discourse relating to AI performance and concerns related to depersonalization, loss of human connection, privacy, bias, and transparency. Trust was found to be higher when AI was supporting rather than replacing health care professionals and was influenced by emotional responses, anthropomorphism, demographic factors, and institutional trust. Furthermore, trust extended beyond algorithms to software interfaces, providers, developers, and governing institutions, highlighting the importance of governance and oversight. Conceptualizations of trust varied widely, and trust was defined through vulnerability, competence, benevolence, and integrity. Different theories identified suggested that trust operates across individual, social, institutional, and technological levels. Finally, trust was closely linked to risk and uncertainty, where perceived risk reduced acceptance, while AI literacy, transparency, and explainability mitigated concerns and fostered trust. Conclusions: Trust in AI is not uniform, and as such, efforts to build and measure trust must account for these nuances to effectively mitigate risk and support informed, ethical AI integration and deployment. On the basis of the findings of this review, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that provides a general understanding of public trust in AI within a health care context that may guide research and policy and practice considerations. Our findings highlight the importance of considering public trust when implementing AI in health care and may support AI communication strategies, policy development, and trustworthy AI development.
title: Trust, Risk, and Uncertainty Surrounding the Use of AI in Health Care: Scoping Review of Studies on Public Perception

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) translate research evidence into actionable recommendations, but their development faces mounting challenges. With dozens of trials and systematic reviews published daily, the traditional 18- to 24-month development cycle struggles to incorporate emerging evidence, and manual screening, synthesis, and quality assessment consume thousands of person-hours per guideline. The resulting knowledge translation pipeline is slow, inconsistent, and quickly outdated. <strong>Objective:</strong> This review aimed to chart the computational methods empirically tested for automating CPG development, the tasks they address, and their evaluation measures, and to map where that evidence is concentrated and where it is absent for living guidelines. <strong>Methods:</strong> The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review framework and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidance. We searched PubMed and Scopus for studies published between January 2001 and December 2025, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching. Eligible studies used automated methods for a guideline development task, reported original research with empirical testing, and gave sufficient methodological detail. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Findings were charted across 4 pillars: retrieval, extraction, encoding, and evaluation. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 47 studies met eligibility criteria, spanning 2001 to 2025, with a marked increase after 2015 and a surge in large language model (LLM) work in 2024-2025. Pillar counts (nonexclusive) were as follows: retrieval, 6; extraction, 15; encoding, 26; and evaluation, 17. In retrieval pillar, query expansion achieved 80% recall, while semantic search tools traded recall for specificity (98%). In extraction, rule-based natural language processing achieved an F-measure of 81.96% for structured clinical actions and 71.75% for patient states, and hybrid ontology methods covered 86% of eligibility criteria; LLMs performed well on structured fields but degraded on interpretive content. In encoding, approaches progressed from formalisms such as Guideline Interchange Format version 3 (GLIF3) and guideline elements model toward Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)–based representation; semiautomated tools assisted guideline encoding, and logic verification detected inconsistencies and coverage gaps missed by human reviewers. In evaluation, LLM appraisers assigned higher Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II (AGREE II) scores than human appraisers, by a mean difference of 12.5% in one study (95% limits of agreement –30.6% to 55.5%; intraclass correlation coefficient 0.753) and by 22 to 60 percentage points across domains in another. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Automation shows promise for bounded, well-structured guideline development tasks, while robust evidence for end-to-end, production-scale living guideline pipelines remains limited. No included study demonstrated a validated pipeline connecting all 4 pillars in an operating guideline program, and evidence on clinical safety, workflow integration, and cost-effectiveness is largely absent. Realizing living guidelines will require interoperability standards such as FHIR, and evaluation in real guideline production rather than retrospective benchmarks.
title: Automation of Living Clinical Practice Guideline Development: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Hypothyroidism is a prevalent endocrine disorder characterized by an insidious onset and nonspecific symptoms, often leading to significant diagnostic delays. While biochemical thyroid function tests (TFTs) are the gold standard, their invasive nature and cost make them impractical for continuous, proactive screening of at-risk populations. Thyroid hormones exert direct chronotropic effects on the cardiovascular system, and their levels are closely correlated with heart rate (HR). Wearable devices capable of continuous HR monitoring offer a novel opportunity for noninvasive, digital phenotype–based detection. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate an AI-assisted system that uses wearable-derived sleep HR data as a digital monitoring tool for individuals at risk of hypothyroidism, helping identify those who warrant further confirmatory thyroid testing. Methods: This retrospective cohort study used 1677 paired observations consisting of sleep HR data and serum TFT results, including free thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels, from 413 participants (mean age 43.1, SD 9.7 y; women: n=314, 76%). Participants wore consumer-grade wearables (Fitbit) that recorded HR and sleep data. Each TFT result was paired with sleep HR data extracted from the 15 consecutive nights preceding the blood test. An AI system was developed using a gradient boosting algorithm (LightGBM) to classify thyroid status by integrating baseline TFT results with statistical and temporal HR features. The model’s performance was evaluated using patient-level leave-one-out cross-validation. To examine the benefit of longitudinal data, performance was compared using 1, 2, or 3 prior paired observations as reference points. Results: To ensure clinical relevance and avoid performance inflation from hyperthyroid cases, we prioritized the analysis of a subset containing only euthyroid and hypothyroid data (n=744 paired observations). In this clinically challenging subset, the system achieved an accuracy of 74.6%, with a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 73.5% using a single-reference data pair. Incorporating longitudinal HR patterns further enhanced performance; using 3 reference pairs improved accuracy to 78.1% (sensitivity 81.8% and specificity 77.7%). In the overall dataset (n=1677 paired observations), the system demonstrated an accuracy of 80.8%, with a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 80.8% using a single-reference pair. Notably, the system achieved high clinical safety by detecting 96.3% of severe overt hypothyroidism cases (free T4 <0.5 ng/dL). Conclusions: This AI-assisted system demonstrates the feasibility of a sensitive, noninvasive longitudinal monitoring tool for hypothyroidism, robustly identifying a high proportion of hypothyroid cases—particularly severe ones—to prioritize at-risk individuals for confirmatory blood tests. Given the predominantly female iatrogenic-withdrawal cohort, prospective sex-balanced validation in primary hypothyroidism is warranted.
title: Harnessing AI for Hypothyroidism Monitoring Using Wearable-Derived Heart Rate Data: Retrospective Cohort Study
